title: Amoebiasis
path: Prevention and Control of Communicable Diseases

headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Amoebiasis
headings.content: Amoebiasis is a prevalent parasitic infection of significant public health importance, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions with developing sanitation infrastructures like Nigeria. Defined medically as an infection caused by the protozoan parasite Entamoeba histolytica, the disease primarily targets the large intestine. While many individuals infected with the organism remain asymptomatic, serving as carriers who silently shed cysts into the environment, others develop symptomatic intestinal illness ranging from mild colitis to severe dysentery. Extraintestinal manifestations can also occur when the parasite breaches the intestinal mucosa and migrates through the portal circulation, most commonly resulting in amoebic liver abscesses. Understanding amoebiasis requires nursing students to appreciate both its gastrointestinal and systemic implications, as patient presentation can vary widely from simple abdominal discomfort to life-threatening sepsis and organ failure. Early recognition, prompt diagnosis, and appropriate nursing interventions are crucial for reducing morbidity and mortality rates associated with this infection in healthcare settings.

headings.title: Causative Agent and Mode of Transmission
headings.content: The causative agent of amoebiasis is Entamoeba histolytica, a protozoan parasite that exists in two distinct forms during its life cycle: the infective cyst and the invasive trophozoite. Cysts are spherical, highly resilient structures capable of surviving for weeks in damp external environments, including contaminated soil and water, due to their protective walls. Trophozoites are the active, motile, and feeding form that colonizes the human gut lumen and causes tissue destruction, but they are fragile and quickly destroyed by gastric acid or environmental exposure outside the host. Transmission of amoebiasis occurs primarily via the fecal-oral route. This happens through the ingestion of food or water contaminated with cysts from human feces, often facilitated by poor personal hygiene, inadequate sanitation, and mechanical vectors like houseflies. In resource-limited communities, consuming unwashed raw vegetables, unboiled water, and failing to practice proper handwashing after defecation and before handling food are major risk factors for acquiring the infection. Nursing students must emphasize health education regarding these transmission pathways to break the cycle of infection within families and communities.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Clinical Manifestations
headings.content: The pathophysiology of amoebiasis begins when ingested cysts excyst in the terminal ileum or colon, releasing active trophozoites. These trophozoites adhere to the colonic mucosal epithelial cells, secrete cytotoxic enzymes, and induce lysis of host cells and leukocytes. This results in the formation of characteristic 'flask-shaped' ulcers in the submucosa of the large intestine. Clinically, intestinal amoebiasis manifests as mild abdominal discomfort, flatulence, and watery or bloody diarrhea containing mucus, a condition clinically known as amoebic dysentery. Systemic symptoms such as low-grade fever, weight loss, and fatigue may also accompany the illness. If trophozoites penetrate the blood vessels of the intestinal wall, they travel via the portal vein to the liver, leading to an amoebic liver abscess. Patients with hepatic involvement typically present with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, point tenderness, and intermittent fever, sometimes accompanied by referred pain to the right shoulder due to diaphragmatic irritation. Recognizing these diverse clinical signs is essential for nurses monitoring patients for disease progression.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Laboratory Investigations
headings.content: Diagnosing amoebiasis accurately requires a combination of clinical evaluation and laboratory investigations. Stool microscopy is a common and accessible diagnostic tool; however, finding Entamoeba histolytica cysts or trophozoites can be challenging because shedding is intermittent, and morphologically identical non-pathogenic species like Entamoeba dispar can confound results. Therefore, multiple stool samples collected on alternate days are often required. Serological tests, such as Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA), are highly sensitive and specific, particularly valuable for diagnosing extraintestinal manifestations like amoebic liver abscesses where stool examinations are frequently negative. Antigen detection tests and Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) assays offer higher specificity to differentiate pathogenic strains from harmless ones. Imaging studies, including abdominal ultrasound, computed tomography (CT) scans, and X-rays, play a vital role in identifying hepatic abscesses or bowel wall thickening. Nurses play a crucial role in preparing patients for these diagnostic procedures, collecting appropriate stool specimens following strict infection control guidelines, and ensuring timely transport to the laboratory.

headings.title: Medical and Nursing Management
headings.content: Medical management of amoebiasis focuses on eliminating both invasive trophozoites and luminal cysts to achieve complete cure and prevent relapse. Treatment typically involves a two-step pharmacological regimen: a tissue amoebicide such as metronidazole or tinidazole to eradicate invasive trophozoites in the bowel wall or liver tissues, followed by a luminal agent like diloxanide furoate or paromomycin to clear any remaining cysts from the intestinal lumen. Nursing management centers on supportive care, monitoring vital signs, and ensuring strict adherence to the medication schedule. Nurses must educate patients about potential side effects of metronidazole, such as a metallic taste, nausea, and a disulfiram-like reaction when alcohol is consumed. Fluid and electrolyte balance must be closely monitored and maintained, especially in patients suffering from severe diarrhea and dehydration, utilizing oral rehydration therapy or intravenous fluids as prescribed. Pain management, comfort measures, and maintaining meticulous personal hygiene to prevent autoinoculation or transmission to others are also fundamental nursing responsibilities in clinical settings.

headings.title: Complications of Amoebiasis
headings.content: If left untreated or diagnosed late, amoebiasis can lead to severe, life-threatening complications requiring urgent surgical and medical interventions. Intestinal complications include toxic megacolon, severe gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and fulminant colitis with bowel perforation, which can cause generalized peritonitis and septic shock. Extraintestinal complications most commonly stem from ruptured amoebic liver abscesses, which can spill necrotic contents into the peritoneal cavity, pleural space, or pericardium, leading to peritonitis, empyema, or cardiac tamponade respectively. Dissemination of the parasite can also result in rare brain or cutaneous abscesses. Nurses must maintain a high index of suspicion and perform meticulous physical assessments to detect early warning signs of complications, such as sudden worsening of abdominal pain, rigid abdomen, board-like guarding, high-grade fever, sudden drops in blood pressure, or respiratory distress. Prompt reporting of these critical findings to the medical team can save the patient's life.

headings.title: Community Prevention and Control Strategies
headings.content: Preventing and controlling amoebiasis at the community level requires a multi-sectoral approach focused on breaking the transmission cycle of Entamoeba histolytica. Public health nurses play a pivotal role in designing and executing community health education programs that promote safe water consumption, such as boiling or treating drinking water with chlorine when safe sources are unavailable. Sanitation infrastructure improvements, including the construction of sanitary latrines and proper sewage disposal systems, are vital to prevent human waste from contaminating soil and water sources. Good personal hygiene practices must be emphasized, particularly rigorous handwashing with soap and clean water after using the toilet, changing diapers, and before preparing or eating food. Additionally, food safety measures must be reinforced, including washing raw fruits and vegetables thoroughly in clean or disinfected water and protecting food from flies and other mechanical vectors. Screening and treating food handlers and asymptomatic carriers in institutional settings also help curb outbreaks and protect vulnerable populations in endemic regions.
